constraint:
The brief, in your words (24 Oct 2026): “extract holdings from multiple broker accounts. Research the top five major brokers and identify the information we need from users to integrate each account. We’ll then display this data in the holdings section.”

Round 1 (19 Oct) picked A · Accounts, then one table, and it is built for Zerodha and Dhan, one account each. This round keeps A’s page and asks how several accounts, two people and five brokers sit on it. Round 1’s canvas is in another organisation, so this round starts a new canvas; its letters carry on from C.
questions:
Open questions, each answerable in a word:

1. Angel One: in, with the MPIN and authenticator code typed each morning and kept never? Or out? (Round 1 asked; no answer yet.)
2. Whose accounts: just “Asha / Ravi / Someone else” names you type, or real Maester users (each signs in themselves)?
3. Groww costs ₹499 a month per account to read holdings, an early-bird price against a listed ₹2,000. Offer it, or list it as not offered?
4. Dhan for a second person: Dhan’s own sign-in (key, secret, a consent each day), or only the Settings connection, one Dhan account per install?

My pick: D. Two people and six accounts are the real shape of the brief, and D is the only direction where whose account it is reads at a glance. E’s round can be added on top later if the morning sign-ins hurt.
shared:
In every direction:

• Several accounts at one broker. Today the database allows one account per broker per workspace, and “Add a broker” hides a broker once it is connected.
• “Whose account is it?” on every add, shown beside every holding, so Zerodha · Asha and Zerodha · Ravi never look alike.
• Each account keeps its own key. Upstox: one app per person. Zerodha: one free app per client ID is the safe reading (its support page and staff differ). Angel One and ICICI Direct: probably one key each.
• One filled button per screen. Today each signed-out account gets a filled “Sign in to …”.
• A share held in several accounts is one row, its parts named, and a part read before its account signed out is starred with the day it was read.
• Figures are synthetic, worked in paise; the product sums them in the engine, never in the page.

rows.title: Today · A as built: one account per broker
rows.note:
Drawn from the code on feat/holdings-dhan (9d1994e, not merged, no PR). Not seen running: it needs a signed-in API with live broker keys.

Measured against a household of six accounts:
• Accounts it can hold: 1 per broker. Zerodha · Ravi can’t be added: the table has a unique index on (workspace, broker), and the picker drops a connected broker.
• Brokers built: 2 (Zerodha, Dhan). Of the top five, Groww, Angel One, Upstox and ICICI Direct have no definition.
• Dhan reads only through the one Settings token, so a second person’s Dhan account can’t exist.
• Held at says “Zerodha 120”: with two Zerodha accounts it can’t say whose.
• Morning cost: every account signs out daily. Six accounts → up to six trips to broker pages, each its own filled button.

Yardstick: accounts 2 → 6; brokers 2 → 5; filled buttons on a bad morning 3 → 1.

rows.title: D · Household, by person
rows.note:
The bet: the household is the unit. People come first, then their accounts.

• “Whose holdings”: Everyone, Asha, Ravi (toggle buttons, aria-pressed). The strip, the accounts and the table follow the choice; weights are of what is shown and the lede says so.
• Accounts are grouped under each person with their value; the first account that needs you is the one filled button.
• The table’s “Held by” sums each person’s parts (Asha 550, Ravi 200); choose a person to see their brokers.

Length: 1.9 desktop screens (Everyone), 1.5 (Ravi); phone 2.3.
Costs: a holder on each account (a name, or a Maester user: question 2); the engine sums per holder; one more control on the page.

rows.title: E · The morning round
rows.note:
The bet: the daily sign-ins are the real cost, so the page leads with them.

• An ink panel at the top: “3 accounts need you this morning”, numbered, each saying what the broker asks for. One action: “Start with Zerodha · Ravi”.
• The round goes broker by broker. A redirect broker sends you back to the panel at the next step; Angel One’s PIN and code are typed in the panel; Groww’s approval opens Groww Cloud and waits for “Read now”. “Skip this one” always works, and what was read stays read.
• Below it, A’s page as built, with accounts named “Zerodha · Asha”.
• With nothing due the panel is gone; it never shows an empty round.

Length: 2.0 desktop screens before the round, 1.0 during it; phone 2.0.
Costs: a round state (which accounts, which step) carried across the broker redirects; the one dark block on the page.

rows.title: F · Accounts as columns
rows.note:
The bet: “where is each share held” is the question, so the table answers it directly.

• One table: a row per company, a column per account (broker, whose, when read), then total quantity, value and weight. The last row is each account’s value.
• A starred column is Friday’s quantities; its header is a button that opens the account above the table: client ID, state, key, and its one action.
• No separate accounts section: the table is the accounts.
• Phone: by company, each with its accounts listed, or by account.

Length: 1.0 desktop screen with six accounts. Past about eight accounts the table scrolls sideways inside its labelled region.
Costs: a wide table component; account management lives in the opened column.

rows.title: Shared · What each broker needs, per account
rows.note:
These come with every direction. The table in Shared 1 is the research, said the way the page would say it; the full page with sources is docs/research/2026-10-24-broker-accounts.md.

• Whose, then which broker, then that broker’s form: numbered steps, the fields, how long a sign-in lasts, what it costs and what you do each day.
• Shared 2: a second Zerodha account needs its own free app with that client ID; the first holder’s developer login can make it, and the second holder signs in each day.
• Shared 4: Groww charges per account (₹499 now, an early-bird price against a listed ₹2,000), said before you save.

rows.title: Shared · The other forms
rows.note: Angel One (question 1) and Groww (question 3) are drawn so you can decide on them. Upstox and ICICI Direct sit side by side here to compare; on the page one form shows at a time, with one filled button.

final.constraint:
Your pick (24 Oct 2026): D. Your change, in your words: “If a user account is automatically locked out, we should display a brief nudge instead of taking up an entire section of the screen.” And: “if we already have the data, we should not ask the user to update it again.”

This page is D · final, with round 4’s colours (gain, loss and G · Highlighter). Earlier rounds sit on the pages behind it. Nothing is built until you say go.
final.questions:
Before the build:

1. The highlight is G · Highlighter here. Keep it?
2. Gain and loss colour Holdings only for now (the rest of the terminal keeps signs only)?
3. The nudge button says “Update 3 accounts”. Fine, or another word?
final.shared:
What changed from D in round 4:

• Signed-out accounts are one line under the title, not a section. Its first words are highlighted; “Update 3 accounts” opens the sign-ins in place (click or tap, Escape closes, focus returns to the button).
• The holdings come straight after the strip, so the first screen is figures. Friday’s parts stay starred: nothing is hidden or asked again.
• Accounts move to the foot of the page with outline buttons only; the nudge holds the one filled button, and only once it is open.
• No nudge when every account was read today.
• First screen given to sign-in prompts, measured: desktop (900px) round 4’s D 48%, this one 8%; phone (844px) 16%, against 41% for round 2’s morning-round panel.

rows.title: D · final
rows.note:
Desktop closed and opened, phone closed and opened.

Opened on desktop, the sign-ins sit in a 2px box under the button, over the page: each account, why it is signed out, and its one action (Sign in to Zerodha, Sign in to Angel One, Open Groww to approve). The first is filled. On a phone they open in place under the line.

Angel One’s MPIN and code are asked for after its button, in the same box, as in round 2.

rows.title: When nothing is due, and the one motion
rows.note:
With every account read today the nudge is gone and nothing is starred.

The nudge’s “simple animation”: the highlighter draws across its first words once on load (240ms) and stays. It never repeats, and under reduced motion it is simply there. DESIGN.md §6 gains a line for it.

round4.constraint:
Your words (24 Oct 2026): “I think the PNL should use distinct colors, such as red and green, that align with the theme. We also need a tertiary color to highlight text or specific areas when required.”

This changes the design system. docs/DESIGN.md §2 today says “No accent colour, no semantic green or red” and that direction is shown by a sign, never a colour. On your go, ADR 0002, DESIGN.md §2 and §5, tokens.css and the design guard change together. Until then nothing in the app changes.
round4.questions:
Questions, each answerable in a word:

1. The highlight: G (recommended), H or J?
2. Gain and loss colour: Holdings only, or every signed change in the terminal (a share’s day change in Research, a reading’s change in Market mood)?
3. The day’s change on Holdings (today versus yesterday’s close): add it as a column now, or later?
round4.shared:
The rules that come with the colours:

• Gain and loss colour only a signed P&L figure and its %. The + or − stays; the colour repeats it.
• Text only: no green or red fills, rows, bars or borders. Unknown stays “—” in ink.
• On an ink panel, the lighter pair (9.63:1 and 8.14:1 on ink).
• The highlight marks something that needs the investor, or a match, in words that already say so. Never the only signal, and at most a few on a screen.
• The illustration yellow stays for drawings only; the highlight is its own token.

rows.title: Palette · gain, loss and one highlight
rows.note:
Researched and computed, not picked by eye (docs/research/2026-10-24-pnl-and-highlight-colours.md).

• Gain #006B55 and loss #BA2C1A pass AA for text on paper (5.53:1 and 5.16:1), for the 14–17px figures in the tables.
• A common red and green (#2E7D32, #C62828) all but merge for deuteranopia (4.3 apart). Leaning the green teal and the red vermilion triples that (12.1) at the same contrast.
• Highlight options: G · Highlighter #F9DC5C, H · Signal orange #FF5F1F, J · Blue pencil #1F4FBF.

rows.title: D with colour
rows.note:
Round 3’s D with the proposal on: P&L and P&L % in gain or loss on every line, the strip’s unrealized P&L too, and G’s highlight on the two things that need you: the lede’s “Three need a sign-in today” and each account’s state when it is signed out or not approved.

E and F take the same colours on the same figures; they aren’t redrawn.

rows.title: The highlight, three ways
rows.note:
The same lines of Ravi’s accounts with each highlight.

I’d pick G: a highlighter is what a person does to a ledger, ink stays fully readable on it, and it stays apart from gain and loss for every kind of colour vision. H competes with the loss colour; J looks like a link.

round3.constraint:
Your words (24 Oct 2026), after round 2: “I’m not getting clear information about which broker’s account holds which positions, and the columns lack profit-and-loss data. This needs to be fixed first before we can proceed.”

So D, E and F keep their ideas, and the holdings table changes in all three. Round 2 is on the next page, unchanged.
round3.shared:
In every direction now:

• Each holding opens into one line per account that holds it: “Zerodha · Asha” with its client ID and when it was read, then its quantity, the broker’s average cost, invested, value, P&L and P&L %.
• The company line adds its accounts up; the total line adds up the page.
• “Show by: Company | Account”. By account gives each account its own ledger and account total.
• The strip shows Invested and Unrealized P&L with its %.
• P&L is unrealized, at Maester’s NSE close, with a sign, never a colour. A part read before its account signed out is starred.

Costs: per-account P&L and P&L % are two new named calculations in the engine, beside holding_cost and holdings_totals. The broker’s average cost is shown as the broker reports it.

rows.title: D · Household, by person, with each account’s P&L
rows.note:
D as in round 2: Whose holdings, and accounts grouped by person. The holdings table now opens each company into its accounts.

HDFC Bank, for example, shows four lines: Zerodha · Asha 120, Zerodha · Ravi 60*, ICICI Direct · Ravi 40, and the total 220, each with its own average cost and P&L.

Choosing Ravi keeps only Ravi’s lines and totals.

rows.title: E · The morning round, with each account’s P&L
rows.note: E as in round 2: the morning round on top, the accounts below. The holdings table is the same company-then-account table as D’s.

rows.title: F · Accounts as columns, with P&L
rows.note:
F keeps a column per account. Each cell gives the account’s quantity and, under it, that account’s P&L % for the share. The last row gives each account’s value and P&L. On the right: total quantity, value, P&L and P&L %.

Average costs and invested amounts don’t fit six columns; they are one click away (choose a column), or under Show by account.

rows.title: Every direction · by account, and the phone
rows.note:
Show by account: one ledger per account, Asha’s first, then Ravi’s, each with its account total and a note when its quantities are Friday’s.

Phone: each company, its P&L, then a line per account with its quantity, average cost and P&L.
